name: Ext3FS File Recovery
description:
Recovering deleted file with Ext2FS is quite easy. With Ext2FS when a file is deleted its meta data (inode) retains its information until the inode is re-used. But with Ext3FS when a file is deleted , inode content is destroyed. So we need to rely on Journal content. It gives you a short window to recover the data. If journal content is also destroyed (normally when you reboot) its very very difficult to recover the data.

Here will explore recovering data from journal details. So let's jump into mini-user guide to recover a delete file from Ext3FS.
Lets create a file called 'giis.txt' with following content this is giis file
So we have a file now. 
$ls -il giis.txt

15 -rw-rw-r-- 2 root root 20 Apr 17 12:08 giis.txt
with contents 
$ cat giis.txt
this is giis file
Now lets go ahead delete the file.
rm giis.txt
rm: remove write-protected regular file `giis.txt'? y
Making sure the file is deleted.
$ ls -il giis.txt
ls: giis.txt: No such file or directory
that's expected error message. Now lets try to recover this deleted file content!

name: Recovering deleted file
description:
We will be using debugfs command to get information like data blocks and inode number. We need to open the root device with debugfs first
debugfs /dev/ubda
Let's check the debugfs command options. Use debugfs to list files -d option

debugfs: ls -d
2 (12) . 2 (12) .. 11 (20) lost+found 2347777 (20) oss
<15> (20) giis.txt

as you can see the deleted filegiis.txt it's different from others It's inode number 15 is surrounded by < and > . Deleted files inode are surrounded by < and >. Now got a chance to recover the file :-)

Since we know that giis.txt files inode number is 15,use it with debugfs's logdump option
debugfs: logdump -i <15>

FS block 1006 logged at sequence 404351, journal block 7241
(inode block for inode 15):
Inode: 15 Type: regular Mode: 0664 Flags: 0x0 Generation: 0
User: 0 Group: 0 Size: 20
File ACL: 0 Directory ACL: 0
Links: 1 Blockcount: 8
Fragment: Address: 0 Number: 0 Size: 0
ctime: 0x48159f2d -- Mon Apr 28 15:25:57 2008
atime: 0x48159f27 -- Mon Apr 28 15:25:51 2008
mtime: 0x4806f070 -- Thu Apr 17 12:08:40 2008
Blocks: (0+1): 10234
No magic number at block 7247: end of journal.

Look carefully you can see the line
Blocks: (0+1): 10234
That's the address (data block) where the content of inode 15 is stored.
So now we know the block address too.
Then what are you waiting for?Go ahead and just use dd command to extract data from that address.(block number)
dd if=/dev/ubda of=/opt/giis_R/txt bs=4096 count=1 skip= 10234
1+0 records in
1+0 records out

where if refers to input device. and of refers to output device. and bs refers to block size.
count indicates 'how many no.of blocks you want to dump?'[we need only one block]
skip tells to skip 10234 blocks from start and dump the next block. Now let's check the content of the txt file
$cat txt
this is giis file

Yes....we got it :-) Recovered a deleted file content!!

name: Summary
description:
Refresh the steps involved in this process :
1)First find inode number of deleted file using debugfs: ls -d
2)Then find data block of inode using debugfs:logdump
3)Finally use data block number with dd command to exact the contents.
